content:
Paying someone is not the first answer when a responsibility has no owner. An empty role feels urgent. A job the church cannot carry, or a ministry the Core Group never learns, costs more than the gap you were trying to close.

Develop people locally, then hire. Define the work, raise volunteers from the Core Group, and use agreed temporary help from a partner church. Pay a role when your leaders can support its cost in a realistic budget. Worship leadership and children's leadership are launch priorities. They are not automatically the first paid jobs.

---

## Start with the Core Group

Leadership for the launch is meant to emerge from the Core Group. The [Key Leadership Roles Overview](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/key-leadership-roles-overview) names the areas a Launch Team needs and tells you to watch who already rises to the surface. Start with a smaller piece of the work.

An unfilled role is a coverage gap. It is not proof that no leaders exist. Character, doctrine, gifting, and relational maturity are judgments for the leaders who know the person. You can record a role's description, time commitment, and desired skills. That record is not employment status and not a pay decision. It does not judge calling, character, fitness, or spiritual health. A leadership candidate signal cannot establish qualification or promote a person. Everyfield does not certify anyone for a role, and it does not gate this hire.

<Callout type="insight">
An empty role means the work is not covered yet. It does not mean the Core Group has failed to produce leaders, and it does not mean you should hire from outside to close the gap.
</Callout>

---

## Name the work before you name a job

Write the responsibility in plain language before you talk about pay. What must be done each week? Which decisions does the person make, and which stay with the Senior Pastor? What skill does the work actually require? How many hours does an honest week take?

That description helps you see the gap. It is not an employment contract, a pay rate, or a verdict on who is called. A church may need worship leadership and children's leadership in place before Launch Sunday. Fill them with developed volunteers or temporary partner help unless the budget can already carry pay.

---

## Borrow help for a set time

If a critical role is still open, do not lower the standard and do not pretend the gap is fine. Someone local can cover the work for a season, or a partner church can lend help. If worship leadership or children's leadership is still missing near a launch date, it may be wise to delay. A launch date also depends on a financial base you can actually see.

Put borrowed help in writing before the person starts. Name the tasks, the end date, who directs the work, who employs the person, and what happens on the end date. Temporary help should leave local people more able to do the work, not dependent on a visitor who does the ministry for them.

<Callout type="tip">
Have a qualified employment attorney review a borrowed-help agreement before the first Sunday. A handshake with a partner church does not settle who employs the person.
</Callout>

---

## Keep volunteer work volunteer

Volunteers belong on this path. They are not unpaid staff. U.S. Department of Labor Fact Sheet 14A says a person generally is not an employee under the Fair Labor Standards Act when the person volunteers freely for public service, religious, or humanitarian objectives, without contemplation or receipt of compensation. Volunteers typically serve part time and do not displace regular employees or do work that would otherwise be performed by regular employees. A paid employee of a nonprofit cannot volunteer the same type of services to that organization.

A specialist gap can stay open, and a willing volunteer can end up carrying a full job. Narrow the responsibility, share it, ask a partner church for temporary help, or delay work you cannot yet do well. Do not pay a wage or a regular stipend, or promise future pay, and still call the person a volunteer.

<Callout type="warning">
If the ministry happens only because one volunteer works like an employee, stop and change the plan. Gratitude does not turn that relationship into volunteer service.
</Callout>

---

## Pay the role when the budget can carry it

A role becomes paid when your leaders can support its cost under a realistic budget. Use [First Year Budget Planning](/wiki/administrative/financial/first-year-budget-planning) and put the full personnel cost on paper, including pay, benefits you promise, and the months when cash will be short.

**Local volunteer.** No pay. The person serves freely while you develop them, and the work stays truly volunteer.

**Partner help.** Pay is whatever the written agreement names. Use it for a set period while local people learn the work.

**Paid staff role.** The church pays from a realistic budget that can still cover a lean month.

A generous Core Group and a budget that can pay a salary are not the same thing. People can give sacrificially while the church still cannot carry another salary. Outside money can make a plant look funded while the Core Group is not yet owning the cost. Count income you can document. Do not treat hoped-for gifts as wages.

Do not create the job because a person is willing to raise personal support. That is not how you fund a first staff role. This guide does not change the Senior Pastor's own support arrangements. Those sit in the budget guide, as documented commitments with their conditions and time limits. A part-time paid role waits for the same budget test. Fewer hours do not skip it.

---

## Ask a lawyer before you hire

This article is not legal advice. Before you hire, classify a worker, or set terms, consult a qualified employment attorney.

Fact Sheet 14A, dated August 2015, says charitable, religious, educational, or similar activities of a nonprofit, where those activities are not in substantial competition with other businesses, do not by themselves make the organization a covered enterprise under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Commercial activity is a separate question. Individual coverage can still apply. The fact sheet's examples include interstate telephone calls, shipping materials to another state, and transporting persons or property to another state. The Wage and Hour Division will not assert individual coverage for isolated, insubstantial time on that work.

For covered nonexempt workers, Fact Sheet 14, revised July 2009, states that the federal minimum wage is not less than $7.25 per hour, effective July 24, 2009. With only some exceptions, overtime is due after 40 hours in a workweek. Your state may require more.

Title VII, as published by the EEOC, defines an employer as a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year, with stated exclusions. Whether that reaches your church is a legal question. The EEOC says religious organizations are permitted to give employment preference to members of their own religion. That exception applies only to institutions whose purpose and character are primarily religious, and it does not allow them otherwise to discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability.

A ministerial exception exists. The EEOC describes it as a First Amendment limit, not a rule written into the discrimination statutes. This article does not say whether it reaches any role. Do not decide it from a job title. When you do hire, use [HR Records and Required Forms](/wiki/administrative/legal/hr-records-and-required-forms) for forms and retention, and [Setting Up Payroll for Church Staff](/wiki/administrative/financial/setting-up-payroll-for-church-staff) for payroll and clergy tax questions. Neither article chooses whom you hire.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 26, 2026. Fact Sheet 14A is dated August 2015, and Fact Sheet 14 was revised in July 2009. Confirm current wage, overtime, coverage, and discrimination rules with the Department of Labor, the EEOC, your state labor agency, and a qualified employment attorney before you hire or set pay.
</Callout>

---

## Check the decision, then stop

Use this list before a responsibility becomes a paid role.

- [ ] The work is written down, including hours and decisions that stay with the Senior Pastor.
- [ ] A local person has been developed, and an empty role was not treated as proof that no leader exists.
- [ ] Partner help has an end date, a named employer, and an attorney's review.
- [ ] No volunteer is carrying the job unpaid, and no employee is volunteering the same work.
- [ ] Documented income can pay the full cost in a lean month.
- [ ] The job does not depend on support the staff member must raise.
- [ ] An employment attorney has reviewed classification, terms, and any claimed exception before an offer.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"And the things which you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also."* — 2 Timothy 2:2 (LSB)
</Callout>

Until the church can carry the cost, keep developing the people who are learning the work.
